prompt: Some cities offer free public transportation. Write an essay arguing whether more cities should do this.
text:
# Should More Cities Make Public Transit Free?

Free public transit is an appealing idea. Nobody pays at the turnstile, buses fill up, and cars come off the road. But a fare is a price, and removing it has costs that someone still has to cover. I think most cities should not make transit free everywhere. They should instead target free or deeply discounted rides at the people and routes where they do the most good.

## The case for free transit

The strongest argument is fairness. Transit riders are disproportionately low-income, and for them a monthly pass can be a real strain. Free fares put money back in the pockets of people who most need it, and they make it easier to reach jobs, clinics and schools. Housing costs have pushed many poorer residents far from city centers, so these trips are often long and necessary.

Free transit also speeds up service. When no one pays, passengers can board at every door and drivers no longer wait while people count coins or tap cards. Kansas City, Missouri, which made its buses free in 2020, reported faster boarding and a drop in conflicts over fares. Fare collection also eats into revenue. In some small systems, the equipment, staff and enforcement cost nearly as much as the fares bring in.

Then there are the benefits beyond the rider. If free service persuades some drivers to leave their cars at home, the city gets less congestion, cleaner air and fewer emissions. Tallinn, Estonia, offers free rides to its residents and has used the policy as part of a broader push toward public life without cars.

## Why free everywhere is the wrong goal

The environmental case is weaker than it looks. Studies of free-fare programs often find that new riders come mostly from people who would otherwise have walked or cycled, not from drivers. That is a gain in access, but it does little for emissions and can crowd buses without removing a single car. Drivers respond mainly to how fast and reliable a trip is, and a zero fare does not fix a bus that comes every forty minutes.

The money matters too. Fares cover a meaningful share of operating costs in many big systems, and in a city like New York or London the loss would run to billions of dollars. Replacing it means higher taxes or cuts elsewhere. If the money comes out of service, the result is the worst possible trade: free buses that are too infrequent to use. Riders consistently rank frequency and reliability above price. A city that spends its limited funds on more frequent buses, dedicated bus lanes and safer stops will usually serve its residents better than one that spends the same money on eliminating fares.

Free service is also poorly targeted. A universal policy gives the same subsidy to a wealthy commuter and a minimum-wage worker. Dependence on a political decision adds risk: when a free program runs into a budget crisis, riders lose the service they had come to rely on, and the city has trouble restoring fares.

## A better approach

Cities can capture most of the equity benefit at a fraction of the cost. Income-based discounts, free passes for students, seniors and job seekers, fare caps that stop charging after a set amount each month, and free service on specific routes or at specific times all reach the people who need help most. Boston has tested free service on selected bus routes, and several cities now offer reduced fares for low-income riders. These programs keep revenue where it is needed while still removing the barrier for those who face it.

Smaller cities with low fare revenue and little congestion are the exception. There, collection costs can swallow most of the fares, and free service is cheap to adopt. Such places have more reason to try it, and their results can teach larger cities what works.

## Conclusion

Transit should be easy to afford, and a city that treats it as a public good is right to do so. But a good system needs frequent, reliable service more than it needs a zero fare, and eliminating fares can pull money away from exactly that. More cities should experiment with free transit in the places where it is cheap or where the need is greatest. Most should put their money into better service and targeted discounts, which help more people for every dollar spent.
